headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 8 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.74–0.95), suggesting that mediterranean diet is associated with a lower risk of bladder cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 73.18%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.

Dietary data from 646,222 study participants, including 3639 incident bladder cancer cases, were analysed.

effect_size.excerpt: lowest diet quality score quintile, HRs (95% CIs) in men was 1.08 (0.86-1.36) for HEI-2015, 1.05 (0.84-1.30) for AHEI-2010, 1.01 (0.80-1.27) for aMED, 1.13 (0.90-1.41) for DASH, and 0.96 (0.76-1.21) for DII®, whereas the corresponding HRs for women were 0.75 (0.53-1.07), 0.64 (0.45-0.92), 0.60 (0.40-0.88), 0.66 (0.46-0.95), and 0.63 (0.43-0.90) with all p values for trend <0.05. The inverse association found in women did not vary by smoking status or race and ethnicity.
